questions.question: What are service objects in Rails and why use them?
questions.title: Service Objects in Rails
questions.direct_answer: A service object is a plain Ruby class that encapsulates one business action ('PlaceOrder', 'SendWelcomeEmail') that doesn't fit in a model (it touches several models, an API, a job) or a controller (it's not HTTP logic). You call it with a class method or call: PlaceOrder.call(user, cart). It keeps controllers thin and models focused on data, and gives the action a single, testable home. The rule: if an action involves multiple models or external calls and isn't CRUD, it's a service object, not fat controller code or model callbacks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know a service object encapsulates one business action (multi-model/external) and is called with .call, keeping controllers thin.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting business logic in controllers (fat controllers) or models (model doing everything), or making a service for trivial CRUD.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: A service object encapsulates one business action (PlaceOrder.call). Use it for multi-model/external actions; keeps controllers thin and models data-focused.

sections.title: A Home for One Business Action
sections.content: A service object is a plain Ruby class that encapsulates one business action — PlaceOrder, SendWelcomeEmail, ImportCsv — that doesn't fit in a model (it touches several models, an external API, a background job) or a controller (it's not HTTP logic). You call it with a class method or call: PlaceOrder.call(user, cart). It keeps controllers thin and models focused on data, and gives the action a single, testable home. The rule: if an action involves multiple models or external calls and isn't CRUD, it's a service object — not fat controller code that mixes HTTP and business logic, and not model callbacks that secretly orchestrate other models.

sections.title: Controller -> Service -> Models
sections.content:
The controller handles HTTP; the service handles the business action; models hold data.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[controller: HTTP + params] --> S[PlaceOrder.call]
  S --> O[Order.create + Charge + Mailer + Job]
  S --> R[returns result to controller]
```

sections.title: A service object
sections.content:
```ruby
# app/services/place_order.rb
class PlaceOrder
  def self.call(user, cart)
    new(user, cart).call
  end

  def initialize(user, cart)
    @user, @cart = user, cart
  end

  def call
    return false unless @cart.items.any?
    order = nil
    ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
      order = Order.create!(user: @user, total: @cart.total)
      @cart.items.each { |item| order.items.create!(item.to_h) }
      Payment.charge(@user, order.total)        # external API
    end
    OrderMailer.with(order: order).receipt_email.deliver_later  # job
    order
  end
end

# Controller stays thin:
class OrdersController < ApplicationController
  def create
    order = PlaceOrder.call(current_user, current_cart)
    if order
      redirect_to order_path(order)
    else
      render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity
    end
  end
end
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Putting business logic in controllers (fat controllers mix HTTP + business).
Stuffing everything into models (model does data + orchestrates + emails).
Making a service for trivial CRUD (over-engineering; use the model).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A service object is a plain class encapsulating ONE business action (PlaceOrder.call).
Use it for multi-model or external-API actions that aren't CRUD.
It keeps controllers thin (HTTP only) and models focused on data.
Call with a class method or call; give the action a single, testable home.
Don't use a service for trivial CRUD (over-engineering) — use the model.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A service object is a plain Ruby class that encapsulates one business action — PlaceOrder, SendWelcomeEmail, ImportCsv — that doesn't fit in a model, because it touches several models, an external API, a background job, or a controller, because it's not HTTP logic. You call it with a class method or call: PlaceOrder dot call of user, cart. It keeps controllers thin and models focused on data, and gives the action a single, testable home. The rule: if an action involves multiple models or external calls and isn't CRUD, it's a service object — not fat controller code that mixes HTTP and business logic, and not model callbacks that secretly orchestrate other models. A common mistake is putting business logic in controllers, which makes fat controllers that mix HTTP and business, and making a service for trivial CRUD, which is over-engineering.
